archetype.name: Retooling (goalie-propped)
archetype.definition: A team that reached the playoffs a year ago but has fallen to the bottom of the league in shot and chance share, and whose above-average goaltending is the main thing keeping games competitive.

report.headline: Goalies keep it close; a team being badly outshot can't keep it there.
report.take:
Philadelphia is 3-7-3, last in the Metropolitan and 29th of 32 on the site. The problem is not bad luck. At 5-on-5 the Flyers own 37.4% of the expected goals (31st) and 42% of the shot attempts (29th). They put 22.7 shots a game on net and allow 31.4, both 30th in the league. Last season this same franchise ran a 50.6% expected-goals share and banked 98 points with four playoff wins. Whatever changed, the territorial game has gone from roughly even to one of the worst in hockey.

What keeps the record from being worse is the crease. Joseph Woll and Dan Vladar are a combined +6.2 goals saved above expected, fifth in the league, and the team's .902 save percentage ranks eighth. That is why a team giving up 30-plus shots a night sits a middling 18th in goals allowed per game. It is also a sharp turnaround from recent years: the goalies were -45.8 GSAx two seasons ago and -6.7 last year. The penalty kill (82.6%, 11th) helps too. The offense has no such prop. At 1.85 goals a game the Flyers rank dead last, and a 25th-ranked power play (16.3%) doesn't rescue it.

The numbers hide how narrow the scoring is. Matvei Michkov has 8 goals on just 19 shots, and Trevor Zegras has 10 points, half of them on the power play. Behind them the shooters are cold: Sean Couturier has no goals on 15 shots, Tyson Foerster 2 on 28, Owen Tippett 1 on 21. Team shooting is 8.1% (31st) against a league norm of 11.3%, so some positive regression is coming. But Michkov's finishing is the one hot number on the roster, and low volume caps what a bounce-back can do. The blueline grades D- and the forwards F. Travis Sanheim logs 25.83 minutes a night with a 40.9% expected-goals share, while most of the defense sits in the low 30s. The one exception is Oliver Bonk at 54.6% in seven games.

The last five games (3-2-0, only 2.2 goals allowed a game) came right after a nine-game losing streak and look like a team finding a floor. That stretch was built on goaltending and tight 3-1 and 3-2 wins, though, not on suddenly winning the shot battle. Until the shot share moves toward where it was last season, this projects as a bottom-five team that steals points when its goalies are excellent.

strengths.title: Goaltending well above expected
strengths.body: Woll (+3.9) and Vladar (+1.8) have both been above average, and the team's 6.2 GSAx ranks fifth. It is the reason a team allowing 31.4 shots a game is mid-pack in goals against. Two goalies doing it at once is more durable than one hot hand, but given this franchise's recent goaltending history, expect some cooling.

strengths.title: A penalty kill that holds
strengths.body: At 82.6% the kill ranks 11th, well above the league's 78.3%. That matters for a team that can't afford to give away special-teams goals. The kill was 77.6% last season, so some of this may be the goalies, but it is a real asset for now.

strengths.title: Recent defensive tightening
strengths.body: Over the last five games the Flyers have allowed 2.2 goals a game, about a goal better than their season rate, and went 3-2-0. It is a small sample, and it leans on the goaltending, but it broke the nine-game skid.

concerns.title: Losing the ice badly at 5-on-5
concerns.body: A 37.4% expected-goals share and a 42% Corsi rank near the very bottom of the league. The team is outshot by several shots a game on both ends of the league average. This is the root problem, and it is a big drop from last season's 50.6%. Neither grade suggests the personnel can fix it quickly: the forwards rate F and the blueline D-.

concerns.title: League-worst offense, thin finishing
concerns.body: At 1.85 goals a game the Flyers rank 32nd, with a 25th-ranked power play. Michkov's 8 goals on 19 shots are carrying a forward group that has 20 goals on 161 shots. Team shooting at 8.1% should rise, but his rate is likely to fall at the same time.

concerns.title: Top pair overmatched in big minutes
concerns.body: Sanheim plays 25.83 minutes a game at a 40.9% xGF share and -8. Drysdale (32.2%) and Seeler (30.9%) are worse. Bonk's 54.6% in seven games is the only defenseman above water, so his role is worth watching.

trend.note: The season opened with a nine-game losing streak before three straight wins and a 3-2-0 last five. That stretch is better on the scoreboard than in the shot share, so the rise is real but shallow.

weekAhead.headline: Two soft spots, then Utah and Minnesota test the shot gap
weekAhead.body:
The week opens with Columbus at home, a fellow bottom-five team on the site (28th). The Blue Jackets' 71% penalty kill (24th) and .887 save percentage give a struggling Flyers power play a rare opening. The next night is Washington on the road, a back-to-back against a 15th-ranked Capitals team shooting 12.4% (9th). Washington's defense has also held defensemen to the third-fewest points relative to expectation, which doesn't help a blueline that barely scores.

The back half is where it turns hard. Utah (5th on the site) and Minnesota (3rd) both come to Philadelphia with top-four expected-goals shares, the exact area where the Flyers are weakest. Utah's goaltending is shaky (.868 save %, 30th) and its kill is 29th, so there are goals to be had if the Flyers can generate shots. Minnesota is a different problem: it allows 21.7 shots a game (2nd) and has an A goaltending grade. Two points from Columbus and Washington, plus one steal behind Woll or Vladar, would be a good week.

keyMatchups.title: Flyers power play vs Utah's kill
keyMatchups.body: Utah's power play leads the league at 38.1%, while its penalty kill sits 29th at 66.7%. Special teams should swing that game both ways. The Flyers' 11th-ranked kill has to hold, and their weak power play has its best chance of the season to convert.

keyMatchups.title: Minnesota's wall against a low-volume offense
keyMatchups.body: Minnesota allows the second-fewest shots a game and has held forwards furthest under expectation of all but two teams. For a Flyers group already 30th in shots, that is close to the worst possible matchup. A low-scoring game that leans on the Flyers' goalies is the most likely script.

keyMatchups.title: Columbus as the must-win
keyMatchups.body: The Blue Jackets rank 28th on the site, with a 97.4 all-situations PDO and a 24th-ranked kill. A home game against them is the clearest chance in the week for Flyers shooters to break their slump.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the Flyers can get their shots-on-goal count anywhere near the opponent's against Utah and Minnesota, or are again relying on Woll and Vladar to cover a 30-plus-shot night.

restOfSeason.body:
The 57-point pace in the sheet is probably too low. Team shooting at 8.1% and a 5-on-5 PDO of 96.5 are bound to climb toward normal, and the goaltending has proven it can steal games. But the underlying shot and chance shares are bottom-three. The saves percentage is also more likely to fall than rise, given how far above recent seasons it sits, and the +1.1 points over goal differential suggests the record already has a little luck in it. Those forces roughly offset, leaving a team that should play closer to a .430-.470 points rate the rest of the way: better than the start, nowhere near last season's 98 points.

What is sustainable is the goaltending being at least average and the penalty kill being solid. What will regress is Michkov's finishing and, likely, some of the save percentage. Unless the forwards and defense start winning possession at something like last year's level, this is a lottery-range team.
swingFactors: Whether the 5-on-5 shot share recovers toward last season's level
Woll and Vladar sustaining above-expected goaltending

confidence.note: Only 13 games, but the shot-share gap is large and consistent enough to trust.
